review: I don't often write reviews, but this one is so atrociously bad I really do feel the need to warn other people to NOT get this game. If you like wandering around and doing nothing, or maybe you want to keep your kid entertained, this might be a good game, but otherwise, it's just absolutely horrible. The camera is some of the worst I've seen in any game, there are MANY MANY bugs, and there is nothing really going on, not to mention just to get to any remotely interesting parts, you just travel around doing nothing on the way there for a looooong time. It's very clear that 90% of it is just filler, and the parts that aren't filler aren't even all that great either. The only thing it has going for it is the art of the game if you like this kind of art. Please do not waste your money on this, its not even worth $1 USD.

[h3]PLEASE NOTE: SPOILERS AHEAD![/h3]

First of all, I would like to emphasize that Paws is not a bad game. But the rating system on Steam does not ask if the game is good or bad but rather if I would recommend it or not. Casually, I probably would recommend it, it's a cute little game. But I am a completionist so I am going to view it from that perspective. And as somebody who strives to complete all achievements in games I play I can not recommend Paws in good concience.

There are several issues I have with the 100% completion of this game. The first thing I noticed were the hunting achievements. You need to catch a certain number of different animals (or their eggs) and in my opinion those numbers are way too high. Let me give you an example: there is one level with swans. You need to eat their eggs from 50 nests. However, there are only around 10 nests in the level. So what you need to do is loot all nests in the level, then quit to the main menu, load your last save file, go through the level again eating the eggs and do this until you reach the target. That's not very fun achievement design in my opinion, especially considering each playthrough only has one save file that is overwritten at the beginning of each new level. So if you do a spoiler-free playthrough and don't know about the achievement you need to play the game from the beginning to reach this level again in order to complete this achievement. For the hunting achievements you need to execute (pun not intended) the same procedure as for the eggs and again, I think the numbers are way too high to be fun because hunting becomes very dull if you've done it a few times. But this is all fine compared to the puffballs achievement which requires you to pop 1000 of them. This just felt ridiculous because what I did to get the majority of the target number is sprinting in circles in a certain spot in a specific level where there are a lot of puffballs. I did this for at least 10 minutes and that didn't even got me all of the puffballs needed.

Another thing that's pretty annoying about the achievements in general is the fact that they don't pop during the game. You only see the notifications for the achievements you've earned after you exit the game. This required me to manually count the animals I caught for the hunting achievements to make sure I would only catch as many animals as I needed and not more.

One other achievement I had trouble with was the one where you need to get all memory fragments in one playthrough. With a guide it's not really hard to find all of the spots you need to interact with but there is one big issue and that's the level with the fox. There are two ways to "beat" this level: get past the fox unharmed which is required to get the fox memory or "die" from the fox and get rescued by the bear which warps you to the next level making it impossible to obtain the memory fragment. On my second playthrough I used a guide to help me find all memories, spirits and items. Sadly, I did die to the fox and the issue here is not the fact that I failed but rather the auto save feature. Since it overwrites your save file after dying you are unable to load the fox level to try again to obtain the fox memory. Which means I needed to do a third playthrough from the very start and since you need to obtain all memory fragements in one run I needed to obtain them all a second time. To prepare for another possible death to the fox I wanted to backup my save file. Usually, you just go into your AppData folder and make a copy of the respective game folder. But obviously it was not as easy in this case because the save data is stored in the Windows registry. I have used the registry before so it wasn't a big deal for me but for people who don't even know what the registry is, how to find it, how to backup something and how to restore it, that's actually not very amazing.

I would also like to mention that the controls and the camera felt a little clunky. Overall, I did enjoy my first playthrough even though I thought it was kinda depressing but I liked it. Completing all achievements however was a pain and I feel like in a short, linear game like this achievements should be designed differently to be fun. Sure, 100% can require a little grind, that's totally fine but I feel like in this game the achievements have not been playtested and feel kinda duct-taped on.

[h3]Long story short:[/h3]
[b]- If you do not care about achievements then play this game, it's very cute!
- If you are a completionist I'd think twice before getting this game.[/b]

Paws is a small but emotionally resonant adventure that stands apart from most traditional games, leaning heavily into atmosphere, tenderness, and visual storytelling rather than mechanical complexity or long-form challenge. Developed and published by Might and Delight, it serves as a companion piece to the studio’s Shelter series, yet establishes a tone and identity all its own. Instead of guiding a parent protecting her young, Paws places you in the body of a vulnerable lynx cub separated from its family. From the very first moments—waking alone on a riverbank after being swept away—the game arises not from survival mechanics but from a journey of reconnection, trust, and quietly unfolding companionship.

What immediately draws you into Paws is its striking art direction. Might and Delight’s distinctive patchwork aesthetic gives the world a handcrafted, almost storybook quality: forests are composed of textured fabrics, lighting shimmers across stylized leaves, and shadows soften the landscape into something dreamlike yet grounded. The world feels intentionally imperfect, slightly abstract but deeply evocative. Combined with a gentle, haunting soundtrack that relies on soft melodies and emotional cues rather than overt themes, the visual and audio design create an atmosphere that feels at once melancholic and hopeful. Rather than overwhelming you with dramatic story beats, the game invites you to slow down and inhabit the forest—watching silhouettes in the trees, listening to distant wildlife, or tracking subtle trails in the snow.

Gameplay in Paws is intentionally minimalistic. Instead of deep combat, complex puzzles, or layered systems, you engage with the world through the senses of a lynx cub: following scent trails, stalking small prey, navigating shallow streams, and learning to move confidently across uneven terrain. Each action is less about challenge and more about immersion—letting you experience the world as the cub does, uncertain but curious. The introduction of a bear cub companion adds warmth to the journey, giving the player moments of shared exploration and simple cooperative mechanics. Together, the two young animals navigate obstacles, help each other reach higher ground, and lend emotional support in an otherwise harsh wilderness. Their relationship becomes the quiet backbone of the narrative, built through small gestures rather than dialogue.

Paws is undeniably short, lasting only a few hours, and this brevity shapes both its strengths and its limitations. As an artistic vignette, the compact runtime enhances the emotional punch: the experience doesn’t overstay its welcome, and every new area feels meaningful. Yet players seeking more expansive gameplay may find themselves wanting more—more levels, more mechanics, more narrative layers. The game occasionally shows its rough edges, particularly in the camera and platforming segments where movement can feel imprecise. Some transitions arrive abruptly, including the ending, which can feel sudden and unresolved depending on the pace at which you play. These issues never derail the experience, but they do highlight that Paws is more of a meditative journey than a fully fleshed-out adventure.

Where the game excels beyond question is in its emotional impact. Even without text or voiced dialogue, Paws communicates themes of loss, fear, protection, and companionship through its environments and through the behavior of its two young protagonists. It is a game built around feelings rather than goals, and its quiet moments linger long after finishing. Whether you’re weaving through dense underbrush, listening to the forest breathe, or simply watching the cubs curl up together in a rare moment of peace, the journey resonates in ways few games attempt. It may not provide mechanical depth, but it offers something rarer—a sense of innocence, vulnerability, and connection.

For players who appreciate narrative lightness, visual artistry, and emotional subtlety, Paws is a memorable and heartfelt experience. It is accessible enough for younger players or newcomers to games, yet meaningful enough for anyone who values atmosphere over systems. Its short runtime may make it feel more like a playable storybook than a traditional video game, but within that structure it succeeds beautifully. Paws is not a grand epic; it is a quiet walk through a dangerous but wondrous world, guided by the fragile courage of a lost lynx cub—and in that simplicity lies its charm.

I found it extremely cute and emotional. I cried during my first play-through and, despite knowing everything that happens, on my 5th l still found the ending gut-wrenching. The music was good, but it only plays for certain sections for limited periods of time. If you stick around and explore, most of the time you'll be without music. Just like Shelter 1 it is a story-line with some, but not much, variability. Like Shelter 2, there are collectables, but it is a manageable amount and much easier to find.

I can say that the description of "Paws: A Shelter 2 game" is not that accurate, because the game is more a relaxing experience than an adventure platformer, and like it said, which deals with loss and friendship. 

The main story focus on a cub lynx that gets separated from the mom and siblings, and is on its way to find its family. The journey is very short, but quite emotive, and involves also getting some food and having a friendly companion.

The atmosphere and soundtrack is really nice and calming, even though I've faced some bugs on the controls and on the background elements.

What actually broke me in "Paws" was the fact I didn't expect to make a choice in the end, and it hit me hard. It made me realize that what matters in life is not reaching our goals, but our journey. [spoiler]When I found my family in the game I was happy for a few moments, but as soon as I noticed that I would have to leave behind alone the cub bear, I just couldn't take it. The bear became a friend and companion during hard times, so it didn't seem right to be selfish and leave it alone because I have reached the end of my journey...[/spoiler]

So yes, I definitely recommend this game <3

[h1]Reseña Alocada: \Paws - Un viaje peludo hacia la aventura\[/h1]

[h2]Resumen[/h2]
¿Alguna vez te has preguntado cómo sería la vida si fueras un adorable cachorro perdido en un mundo gigantesco? ¡Bienvenido a \Paws\! Este juego te mete en la cola… digo, en la piel de un pequeñín de cuatro patas con más aventuras de las que podrías imaginar en tu ordenador. 

[h2]Aspectos importantes e interesantes[/h2]
- **Gráficos y Ambientación**: Prepárate para quedarte con la boca abierta más tiempo que un cachorro viendo una salchicha girar en el microondas. Los escenarios son tan preciosos que te dan ganas de imprimirlos y colgarlos en la pared.
- **Historia Emocionante**: Más envolvente que una maratón de series en domingo, la trama de \Paws\ es una montaña rusa de emociones con más subidas y bajadas que mi cuenta bancaria en época de rebajas.
- **Múltiples Finales**: Así es, porque un paseo nunca es suficiente, puedes replantear tus decisiones para ver diferentes finales. ¡Porque a quién no le gusta ser un cachorro con crisis existenciales!

[h2]Aspectos por mejorar[/h2]
- **Voces**: Estamos buscando desesperadamente dónde dejaron los diálogos porque, a menos que los ladridos cuenten como lenguaje alienígena avanzado, aquí hay silencio absoluto.
- **Dificultad/IA**: Tan predecible como las comedias románticas de los 90, no esperes mucha resistencia por parte de los \enemigos\. Más bien es como jugar al escondite con un niño de tres años… sabes que ganarás.

While this is a very beautiful game and the story it tells is heartwarming and bittersweet, that's all that it is. In case you didn't know, Paws is a spin-off to the game, Shelter 2. It serves as a prequel of sorts through the eyes of the lynx cub Inna. Inna grows up to be the first lynx mother you can play in Shelter 2.
That being said, if you are looking for another Shelter 2 in this game or hoping for the experience of Shelter 2 through the eyes of a cub instead of the mother, then this is not the game for you. It is an exceptionally short 3D platformer through which you must travel. 

There are barely any unique levels through which you traverse and the whole thing just feels more like a drudge through scripted events than an actual interactive puzzle platformer. While I loved this game when it first released, I was ultimately disappointed with how far it strayed from Shelter 2's innovation of the Shelter series thus far. No other game in the series (except perhaps Meadow but only barely) comes even close to capturing what Shelter 2 created for me and many others.. 

So, unless you're looking for a one and done, extremely short little story that is more scripted events than it is puzzles, this might be for you. If you're looking for Shelter 2 but as a cub, this game will let you down just like it did for me.

I love M&D as a game company. They gave me the Shelter series which to this day remains one of my favorites. However, I do wish they'd learn from Shelter 2 and make any future entries to the series more similar to it than Paws. Stay away from the scripted, confusing to navigate tunnel vision story and open things up to a beautiful world of possibilities and replayability.
